physical_harm: Death caused by a single stab injury to the chest
number_of_offences: Charged with one offence, upheld as one offence
premeditation_planning: Yes, the court found premeditation and planning
motive: To avenge his humiliation at the hands of the deceased
key_evidence_accepted: The evidence of the case makes it clear that Section 304 (Part II) IPC is not attracted. The nature of weapon used and the part of the body where the blow was struck, which was a vital part of the body, helps in proving beyond reasonable doubt, the intention of the appellant to cause the death of the deceased.
witness_credibility: The High Court found the testimony of PW-1 Paulose who is the eyewitness and PW-3 Havildar Indrpal to whom the dying declaration was given by the deceased, is reliable.

legal_representation.accused: K.K. Mani, Ankit Swarup and K, Lakshminarayan
legal_representation.state: Brijender Chahar, R.Balasubramaniyam, Naresh Kaushik, Anil Katiyar and D.S. Mahra

investigation_status: FIR lodged, charge-sheet prepared, trial completed
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the accused caused the death of the deceased through a deliberate act, using a sharp kitchen knife to stab him on the chest, which is a vital part of the body. The accused had time to plan and deliberate, and the weapon used was dangerous enough to cause death. The prosecution contended that the act was intentional and fell under Section 302 IPC, not Section 304 (Part II).
defence_argument: The defence argued that the accused acted under grave and sudden provocation due to the deceased's abuse, and therefore, the offence fell under Exception I to Section 300 IPC. They also contended that the single stab injury indicated an absence of intention to cause death, thus making Section 304 (Part II) applicable instead of Section 302.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the legal principle that the intention to cause death is the key factor in determining whether an act constitutes murder under Section 302 IPC. The court emphasized that the nature of the injury, the part of the body struck, and the weapon used are critical in assessing the offender's intent.
precedent_relied_upon: Mancini v. Director of Public Prosecution (1942) A.C. 200; Rex v. Lesbini (1914) 3 K.B. 1116; State of Rajasthan v. Dhool Singh (2004) 12 SCC 546; Virsa Singh v. State of Punjab AIR 1958 SC 465; Anil v. State of Haryana (2007) 10 SCC 274
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence of life imprisonment was imposed because the court found that the accused had the intention to cause death, and the act was deliberate, not impulsive. The court rejected the defence's argument that the act fell under Exception I to Section 300 IPC or Section 304 (Part II).
